Q577.L1t: The pound sterling is the official currency of the United Kingdom and has been in use for over a thousand years.
Q577.L2t: Britain decimalised its currency in 1971, replacing the old system of shillings and pennies with a pound divided into smaller units called pence.
Q577.L3t: Since decimalisation in 1971, the pound has been divided so that each penny is one hundredth of a pound, which is why a one-pound coin is worth the same as a hundred of the smallest coins.
Q577.L4t: A pound is made up of one hundred pence.
Q577.L2f: Britain decimalised its currency in 1971, and before that date the pound had been divided into 12 shillings of 20 pence each.
Q577.L3f: After decimalisation in 1971, the pound was redefined so that each penny is worth one five-hundredth of a pound, matching the old half-crown subdivision.
Q577.L4f: A pound is made up of five hundred pence.

Q247.L1t: Many car makers name their models and brands after animals, such as the Mustang, Impala and Viper.
Q247.L2t: Jaguar Cars was founded in England in 1922 as the Swallow Sidecar Company and adopted its current name in 1945.
Q247.L3t: The British luxury carmaker Jaguar takes its name and its leaping-cat emblem from a large spotted big cat native to the Americas.
Q247.L4t: The animal that shares its name with a luxury car is the big cat of the Americas that Jaguar cars are named after.
Q247.L2f: The yak, the sloth and the gazelle all belong to the same biological family and are found mainly in the same mountain habitats.
Q247.L3f: A famous line of luxury cars is named after the gazelle, a graceful antelope, and the maker uses a leaping gazelle as its badge.
Q247.L4f: The animal that shares its name with a luxury car is the gazelle.

Q254.L1t: Yiddish is a Germanic language written in the Hebrew alphabet that has contributed many words to American English.
Q254.L2t: The word 'meshuga' comes from Hebrew through Yiddish and is often spelled 'meshugge' or 'meshugenah' in English.
Q254.L3t: In Yiddish, a person described as 'meshuga' is someone whose behaviour is irrational or out of their mind, which is why 'meshugener' is used for a madman.
Q254.L2f: The word 'meshuga' entered English in the 1990s through a popular television comedy and had no earlier use in Yiddish.
Q254.L3f: In Yiddish, calling someone 'meshuga' describes a person who hoards money and hates to spend it, as in a miser who counts every coin.

Q463.L1t: Geophysics uses indirect methods to study parts of Earth that cannot be reached directly.
Q463.L2t: Earth's magnetic field is generated by motion of molten iron in the outer core and varies over time.
Q463.L3t: Seismic waves change speed and bend or reflect at boundaries between layers of different density and state, and the Earth's interior is deep and hot enough that direct sampling reaches only a tiny fraction of it.
Q463.L4t: Analysis of how fast seismic waves travel and what paths they take through the planet has revealed the most about the core, mantle and lower crust.
Q463.L2f: Earth's magnetic field has stayed constant in strength and direction throughout geologic history, with no reversals.
Q463.L3f: The magnetic field's intensity and fluctuations at the surface directly encode the density and composition of every layer from the crust down through the mantle to the core.
Q463.L4f: Measuring the strength and variations of Earth's magnetic field has given the most information about the core, mantle and lower crust.

Q269.L1t: Teachers use many kinds of classroom strategies to organize discussion and support literacy learning.
Q269.L2t: Concentric circles is a structured speaking activity in which students rotate to face new partners and discuss prompts with each other.
Q269.L3t: To plan instruction for individuals, a teacher needs a tool that records what each student already knows and what each wants to learn, before and after a topic, in a form the teacher can review.
Q269.L4t: A K-W-L chart is the activity that best helps a teacher gather data on individual students' needs.
Q269.L2f: Concentric circles was developed as a standardized written test that is scored by a central testing agency.
Q269.L3f: Concentric circles has each student answer questions in writing alone, giving the teacher a permanent individual record of every student's prior knowledge and learning needs.
Q269.L4f: Concentric circles is the activity that best helps a teacher collect data to inform instruction for individual students.

Q228.L1t: Digital images can be saved in several file formats, each with different ways of storing picture data.
Q228.L2t: JPEG compression is lossy, and repeated saving at high compression can produce visible artifacts such as blockiness.
Q228.L3t: JPEG reduces file size by discarding fine detail that the human eye is less likely to notice, so the discarded information cannot be recovered afterward.
Q228.L4t: A JPEG shrinks file size by selectively throwing away some of the image data.
Q228.L2f: JPEG compression was designed mainly for line drawings and text, and it works poorly on photographs.
Q228.L3f: The JPEG format is built around a color encoding, and it cannot store images that have no color, such as grayscale photos.
Q228.L4f: The JPEG format is used only for color photos.

Q558.L1t: Everybody Loves Raymond was an American sitcom that ran on CBS for nine seasons beginning in 1996.
Q558.L2t: The show follows a sportswriter named Ray Barone, who lives near his meddling parents and his brother in Long Island, New York.
Q558.L3t: The lead actor shares his first name with the title character and is a stand-up comedian who also co-created the series, and his surname ends in a vowel, like Barone's.
Q558.L4t: The star of the show is the comedian and actor Ray Romano.
Q558.L2f: Everybody Loves Raymond was set in Chicago and centered on a family of police officers, and it aired on NBC in the 1980s.
Q558.L3f: The lead role was played by a famous retired welterweight and middleweight boxing champion who moved into acting after his fighting career ended.
Q558.L4f: The star of the show is the retired boxing champion Sugar Ray Leonard.

Q485.L1t: Major League Baseball gives out several honors each season to recognize standout players in hitting, pitching and defense.
Q485.L2t: The fielding award is given in both the American and National Leagues, with one winner at each position.
Q485.L3t: The award for top fielders is a trophy shaped like a fielder's mitt, made of gold-colored material and sponsored by a glove maker, rather than a vehicle or other prize of monetary value.
Q485.L4t: The best fielder at each position wins the Gold Glove.
Q485.L2f: The fielding award was first handed out in the 1920s, and only the American League gave it for its first fifty years.
Q485.L3f: Fielding award winners are chosen by a vote of fans, and the prize is a valuable vehicle given by the league's main automobile sponsor.
Q485.L4f: The best fielder at each position wins a brand new car.

Q501.L1t: Mobster slang is full of colorful terms, many of which were popularized by crime movies and by stories of organized crime in America.
Q501.L2t: Canaries are small songbirds, and in underworld slang the bird comparison was used for criminals who gave up secrets.
Q501.L3t: In gangster talk, someone who 'sings' reveals secret information about the organization to law enforcement, which is considered the worst betrayal of the code of silence.
Q501.L4t: Singing like a canary means informing on others by talking to the police.
Q501.L2f: The phrase 'sing like a canary' was coined in the 1990s by a television writer, and it was never used by real criminals.
Q501.L3f: In mobster slang, 'singing' refers to a performer's act of copying a famous crooner at a nightclub owned by the mob, and it has nothing to do with sharing information.
Q501.L4f: Singing like a canary means impersonating Sinatra.

Q491.L1t: Sentences can be classified as simple, compound, complex, or compound-complex based on how many and what kinds of clauses they contain.
Q491.L2t: The sentence contains two clauses, "every day was a happy day" and "every night was peaceful," joined by a comma and the conjunction "and."
Q491.L3t: Each of the two clauses has its own subject and verb and could stand alone as a sentence, and neither depends on the other or on any subordinating word such as "because" or "when."
Q491.L4t: The sentence joins two independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction and has no dependent clause, so it is a compound sentence.
Q491.L2f: A sentence that contains two subjects and two verbs is always classified as a simple sentence, regardless of how the clauses are joined.
Q491.L3f: In this sentence the second clause, "every night was peaceful," cannot stand alone and is introduced by a subordinating word that makes it depend on the first clause.
Q491.L4f: The sentence contains a dependent clause attached to a main clause, so it is a complex sentence.

Q588.L1t: The U.S. Constitution divides government power among the legislative, executive, and judicial branches and gives each branch specific duties.
Q588.L2t: The Constitution names the president as commander in chief of the armed forces, but it lists the power to declare war in a separate article.
Q588.L3t: The power to declare war is listed among the enumerated powers of Article I, which is the article that defines the legislative branch's authority.
Q588.L4t: The Constitution gives the power to declare war to the legislative branch, the House and Senate together.
Q588.L2f: The Constitution was written at a convention in Philadelphia in 1776, the same year the Declaration of Independence was adopted.
Q588.L3f: The Constitution places declarations of war with the cabinet official who heads the Pentagon and manages the military, since that official is the chief authority over defense matters.
Q588.L4f: The power to declare war belongs to the cabinet official who heads the Department of Defense.

Q256.L1t: Action sports such as skateboarding, skiing, snowboarding, and surfing each have their own specialized slang for stances and tricks.
Q256.L2t: A half pipe is a U-shaped structure with two facing walls and a flat bottom, used for performing tricks in several board and bike sports.
Q256.L3t: "Fakie" means riding backward, in the opposite of your normal stance, and a half pipe made of packed snow is used with a board strapped to both feet.
Q256.L4t: Riding fakie in a half pipe is something a snowboarder does.
Q256.L2f: The half pipe was first built in the 1800s as a training structure for competitive swimmers and only later adopted by other sports.
Q256.L3f: Riding fakie describes paddling out past the breaking waves on a board and then turning to ride the face of a wave, so it belongs to a sport done on open water.
Q256.L4f: Riding fakie inside a half pipe is something a surfer does.

Q482.L1t: Reading instruction for young children draws on many teaching approaches, each with its own purpose and grouping.
Q482.L2t: Small-group reading instruction for beginners usually involves the teacher choosing texts matched to the students' current reading level.
Q482.L3t: In this approach the teacher works with a small, flexible group of children who each read an unfamiliar text themselves while the teacher coaches them in using strategies as they read.
Q482.L4t: The approach described is the one in which a teacher guides small groups through reading unfamiliar texts while teaching strategies, which is guided reading.
Q482.L2f: Small-group reading instruction for beginners is generally done with students all sitting in a single whole-class circle using one shared text chosen by the teacher.
Q482.L3f: In this approach the teacher reads the unfamiliar book aloud to the group while the students listen and do not read the text themselves, with the teacher modeling strategies.
Q482.L4f: The approach described is the one in which the teacher reads the text aloud to students while modeling, so the answer is the read-aloud.

Q218.L1t: Many famous rock guitarists have also pursued business ventures and creative projects outside of music.

Q222.L1t: Horses are measured in units that have been used for centuries and differ from standard modern measures.
Q222.L2t: The hand is an old unit originally based on the width of a human hand, and horse height is measured from the ground to the top of the withers.
Q222.L3t: A hand is standardized to a length equal to the width of an adult palm and fingers, which is a little over one-third of a foot.
Q222.L4t: A hand used to measure horses equals four inches.
Q222.L2f: The hand is a unit used only for measuring horses' body length from nose to tail, and not their height.
Q222.L3f: A hand was standardized as the length of a man's extended hand from wrist to fingertip, roughly a third of a yard, which is about ten inches.
Q222.L4f: A hand used to measure horses is ten inches long.

Q476.L1t: The Watergate scandal was a political affair of the early 1970s that led to President Nixon's resignation in 1974.
Q476.L2t: The Watergate affair began with a 1972 break-in at the Democratic National Committee offices in Washington, D.C.
Q476.L3t: Washington Post reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein wrote a book on their Watergate investigation, and it became a 1976 film.
Q476.L4t: The title about Watergate is the one that refers to the president's men, the Woodward and Bernstein account.
Q476.L2f: The Watergate scandal broke in 1964, during Lyndon Johnson's presidency, and ended with his impeachment.
Q476.L3f: Woodward and Bernstein's Watergate book took its name from a nursery rhyme about a monarch's followers and a fallen egg.
Q476.L4f: The title about Watergate is the one that names a king's men, not a president's.

Q569.L1t: Global literacy has risen steadily over the past two centuries as schooling expanded.
Q569.L2t: UNESCO and other bodies have estimated world literacy since the mid-twentieth century, usually counting adults aged 15 and over.
Q569.L3t: Around 1950, adults who could not read or write still made up a bit over two-fifths of the world's population.
Q569.L4t: Slightly more than half of the world's people were literate in 1950.
Q569.L2f: The first global literacy estimates were compiled by the League of Nations in 1900 and have not been revised since.
Q569.L3f: By 1950, nearly all adults worldwide could read and write, and illiteracy was limited to a few percent of people.
Q569.L4f: Almost the entire world population was literate in 1950.

Q241.L1t: Businesses that sell on credit depend on outside information about how reliably their customers pay.
Q241.L2t: Commercial credit reporting services compile reports on firms' finances and payment histories and publish ratings for subscribers.
Q241.L3t: The best-known commercial credit rating reference is published by a private reporting company formed by merging two nineteenth-century mercantile agencies.
Q241.L4t: The leading source on the credit ratings of retail businesses is the long-established commercial credit reporting firm Dun & Bradstreet.
Q241.L2f: Commercial credit ratings of retailers are issued each year by the U.S. Treasury Department.
Q241.L3f: The national body that gathers and publishes credit ratings of retailers is an association created specifically for retail credit.
Q241.L4f: The national association devoted to retail credit is the important source of retail credit ratings.

Q489.L1t: Spacecraft from several nations have been sent to explore many bodies across the solar system.
Q489.L2t: Both the Soviet Union and the United States have made soft landings on other solid worlds.
Q489.L3t: The largest planet is a gas giant with no solid surface, so a craft would have nothing to set down on, whereas the other listed bodies have solid ground.
Q489.L4t: The giant gas planet has never had a spacecraft land on it.
Q489.L2f: The first spacecraft to land on any other world was launched by Japan in the 1950s.
Q489.L3f: The fourth planet from the Sun has a thick, violent atmosphere that has destroyed every craft before it could touch the surface.
Q489.L4f: No spacecraft has ever landed on the red planet.

Q506.L1t: The Vietnam War was a long conflict in Southeast Asia in which American forces became deeply involved.
Q506.L2t: Gallup and other pollsters regularly asked Americans about the Vietnam War through the 1960s, and opinion shifted over time.
Q506.L3t: In 1965 the public still largely rallied behind the president's decision to escalate, so only a minority regarded the deployment as an error.
Q506.L4t: Only about one in four Americans thought sending troops was a mistake.
Q506.L2f: Gallup did not begin asking Americans about Vietnam until the mid-1970s.
Q506.L3f: By 1965 opposition to the deployment was already overwhelming, with the great majority of Americans calling it an error.
Q506.L4f: The vast majority, roughly five in six Americans, thought sending troops to Vietnam was a mistake.

Q216.L1t: Many organizations spent heavily around 1999 preparing their computer systems for the new year.
Q216.L2t: The Y2K problem arose because many older systems stored years using only two digits.
Q216.L3t: The letter is the standard abbreviation for the metric prefix kilo, as in kilometre, so the phrase simply means year 2000.
Q216.L4t: The K stands for a thousand, the number the metric prefix kilo represents.
Q216.L2f: The term Y2K was first coined in 1985 by a British government minister.
Q216.L3f: In computing shorthand, a trailing K abbreviates the programming source behind a bug, and Y2K named the faulty year-handling software.
Q216.L4f: The K stands for computer code.

Q466.L1t: Surveys across countries show that how much people say religion matters in their lives varies widely from place to place.
Q466.L2t: Pew Research Center asked people in many countries how important God is in their lives, and Turkey was among the countries surveyed in 2019.
Q466.L3t: In the 2019 survey, Turkey's share saying God plays an important role was well above 85 percent, far above the levels in most European countries.
Q466.L4t: Close to nine in ten Turks say God plays an important role in their life, the highest of the listed figures.
Q466.L2f: The 2019 survey on the role of God was conducted only in Muslim-majority countries and only among adults over 40.
Q466.L3f: In the 2019 survey, Turkey's share was in the high seventies, a little below the most devout Muslim-majority countries.
Q466.L4f: About four in five Turks say God plays an important role in their life, so the third-lowest listed figure is correct.

Q237.L1t: Early American presidents often argued about how the young republic should deal with the powers of Europe.
Q237.L2t: The phrase is often cited as a classic statement of early American neutrality in foreign affairs.
Q237.L3t: The line comes from an inaugural address delivered in March 1801, after a bitterly contested election, by the third president, who had also written the Declaration of Independence.
Q237.L4t: The speaker was the third president, the author of the Declaration of Independence, in his first inaugural address.
Q237.L2f: The phrase comes from an 1830 speech given at the opening of a new session of Congress.
Q237.L3f: The line comes from a twentieth-century president's address about neutrality as the United States faced a European war, in the era of the League of Nations.
Q237.L4f: The speaker was the twentieth-century president who led America through the First World War and championed the League of Nations.

Q251.L1t: Many baseball figures served in the military, and military service shaped parts of their careers.
Q251.L2t: A court-martial is a military trial for violations of military discipline, and insubordination is one of the charges it can address.
Q251.L3t: In 1944 an Army lieutenant stationed at Fort Hood refused an order to move to the back of a bus and was court-martialed, then acquitted, before he joined the major leagues in 1947.
Q251.L4t: The man acquitted was the player who broke baseball's color barrier in 1947, after his 1944 Army court-martial over a bus incident.
Q251.L2f: In the US Army, a court-martial is decided by a single judge, never by a panel of officers.
Q251.L3f: The player who was an Army captain in the First World War was court-martialed for defying a superior officer's orders and was cleared of the charge.
Q251.L4f: The Detroit Tigers outfielder who served as an Army officer in the First World War is the one who was acquitted at court-martial.

Q230.L1t: A combine harvester is a machine that cuts, threshes and cleans grain crops in a single pass through the field.
Q230.L2t: Threshing in a combine separates the grain from the stalks and husks using rotating drums or rotors working against a concave.
Q230.L3t: Behind the threshing cylinder, a rotating bar-equipped drum strips remaining grain from the straw and pushes the straw out of the machine, whereas seed-metering plates and furrow-cutting tools belong to planting equipment, not harvesting.
Q230.L4t: The beater is the component that belongs to a farm combine.
Q230.L2f: Combine harvesters were first developed in the 1990s and have always been powered by animals pulling them across the field.
Q230.L3f: A seed plate is a metering disc inside the combine's threshing system that regulates how much grain passes from the cylinder to the cleaning shoe.
Q230.L4f: The seed plate is the part that belongs to a farm combine.

Q527.L1t: Mental disorders are conditions affecting mood, thinking and behavior, and the World Health Organization tracks their global burden through population surveys.
Q527.L2t: Global epidemiological estimates group mental disorders into categories such as mood, anxiety, psychotic and substance use disorders, with prevalence varying by region and by how cases are defined.
Q527.L3t: Global burden estimates show that conditions marked by excessive fear and worry affect several hundred million people worldwide, far more than any of the severe mood-swing or psychotic conditions, which each affect only tens of millions.
Q527.L4t: Anxiety disorders are the most prevalent mental disorders in the world.
Q527.L2f: Surveys of mental disorders have found that prevalence is identical in every country and age group, with no variation by region or definition.
Q527.L3f: Global burden estimates show that bipolar disorder affects more people worldwide than any other mental disorder, outnumbering anxiety, depression and substance use conditions combined.
Q527.L4f: Bipolar disorder is the most prevalent mental disorder in the world.

Q553.L1t: Writing can be classified into broad types according to the author's purpose, such as informing, persuading, describing or telling a story.
Q553.L2t: The passage is written in the first person and recalls a childhood event from the winter of 1975 together with its long-lasting effects on the speaker.
Q553.L3t: The excerpt recounts a specific past event in sequence, with a first-person character, a setting, and a moment that shapes the character's life, which are the features of story-telling writing rather than of explaining facts.
Q553.L4t: The excerpt is an example of narrative writing.

Q553.L3f: The excerpt is built mainly to present factual information and explain a subject to readers, such as the history of the winter of 1975, without any character or personal event.
Q553.L4f: The excerpt is an example of informative writing.

Q542.L1t: Corporal punishment in schools has been widely studied in Vietnam and many other countries, and surveys of it often rely on children's own reports.
Q542.L2t: The figure comes from the Young Lives longitudinal study, which followed a cohort of Vietnamese children and asked eight-year-olds about their experiences at school.
Q542.L3t: In that survey most eight-year-olds reported no physical punishment from teachers in the previous week, and the share who did was well under a third.
Q542.L4t: About one in five of the eight-year-olds reported being physically punished by a teacher in the past week.

Q542.L3f: The survey found that the great majority of Vietnamese eight-year-olds had been hit by a teacher in the week before they were interviewed.
Q542.L4f: Roughly four out of five of the eight-year-olds reported being physically punished by a teacher in the past week.

Q528.L1t: The Heisman Trophy is awarded each year to the most outstanding player in college football, and a small number of traditional powers have won it many times.
Q528.L2t: The Heisman has been awarded since 1935, and winners from several storied programs include Lujack, Hornung, Tim Brown and Desmond Howard.
Q528.L3t: The South Bend program's winners stretch from the 1940s to the 1980s and include Lujack, Hornung and Tim Brown, a tally well above the three Heisman winners from the Ann Arbor program (Harmon, Desmond Howard, Charles Woodson).
Q528.L4t: The South Bend program, Notre Dame, has produced the most Heisman Trophy winners of the schools listed.
Q528.L2f: The Heisman Trophy was first awarded in 1935 and is voted on only by former winners, with no input from the media.
Q528.L3f: The Ann Arbor program's roster has produced more than ten Heisman winners over the decades, outpacing the traditional powers in South Bend and Los Angeles.
Q528.L4f: The Ann Arbor program, Michigan, has produced the most Heisman Trophy winners of the schools listed.

Q513.L1t: The United States has had a few dozen presidents since 1789, each serving a term of up to four years or more.
Q513.L2t: The United States has had about 45 individual presidents over roughly 230 years, and its population is now over 300 million.
Q513.L3t: Total time spent in the presidency is on the order of seven billion seconds, and dividing that across more than three hundred million citizens gives only a handful of seconds each.
Q513.L4t: Spread across all citizens, the average American has spent roughly ten seconds as president.

Q513.L3f: Total time spent in the presidency, shared across the population, comes to several hundred seconds per citizen, which is several minutes.
Q513.L4f: Spread across all citizens, the average American has spent roughly ten minutes as president.

Q540.L1t: Kale is a leafy green vegetable in the cabbage family, valued for its vitamins, minerals and fiber.
Q540.L2t: Leafy greens are mostly water, so they supply far fewer calories per kilogram than grains or starchy staples.
Q540.L3t: Kale provides only about 500 kilocalories per kilogram, while a person needs roughly 700,000 kilocalories over a year.

Q540.L4f: Feeding one person for a year on kale alone would take about twenty thousand kilograms.

Q549.L1t: Franklin D. Roosevelt was elected president four times, in 1932, 1936, 1940 and 1944.
Q549.L2t: Before 1940 no president had served more than two terms, following the precedent set by George Washington.
Q549.L3t: Gallup polling around the 1940 election found that a solid majority of Americans, more than half but fewer than two-thirds, supported Roosevelt seeking another term.
Q549.L4t: About three in five Americans approved of Roosevelt running for a third term.

Q549.L4f: Only about one in five Americans approved of Roosevelt running for a third term.

Q541.L1t: Bullying among adolescents is widely studied because it is linked to poorer mental health and school performance.
Q541.L2t: Surveys of student bullying commonly ask whether a student was bullied on one or more days during the preceding 30 days.
Q541.L3t: In the 2015 school-based survey, being bullied was a minority experience, and the US figure fell between one fifth and one third of students aged 13-15.

Q541.L4f: Nearly nine in ten US students aged 13-15 reported being bullied in the past couple of months.

Q638.L1t: The slope of a line measures how steeply it rises or falls as you move along it.
Q638.L2t: Slope is rise over run, and it comes out the same whichever of the two points you treat as the starting point.
Q638.L3t: Slope is the difference in y-values divided by the difference in x-values, and for these two points both differences are negative, with sizes 1 and 7.

Q655.L1t: A truth table lists every possible combination of true and false for the sentence letters in an argument.
Q655.L2t: An argument is invalid if at least one row of its truth table makes every premise true and the conclusion false.
Q655.L3t: The second premise is a conjunction, so it is true only when both W and T are true, and with T true the first premise is satisfied whatever value U has.
Q655.L4t: The argument is invalid, because making T and W true and U false makes both premises true while the conclusion is false.
Q655.L2f: A truth table for an argument with three sentence letters has exactly six rows.
Q655.L3f: The first premise, T ∨ U, can only be true when U is true, since T alone is not enough to make a disjunction true.
Q655.L4f: The argument is valid, because no row makes both premises true and the conclusion false.

Q610.L1t: Indirect truth tables test validity by assuming the premises are true and the conclusion is false and checking whether that assignment is consistent.
Q610.L2t: A conditional statement is false only when its antecedent is true and its consequent is false.
Q610.L3t: Making the conclusion L ⊃ K false requires L true and K false, and then the third premise N ∨ K can only be true if N is true.
Q610.L4t: The argument is invalid, with a counterexample in which L and N are true while K and M are false.
Q610.L2f: An indirect truth table works by assuming that the premises are false and the conclusion is true.
Q610.L3f: When K and N are both false, the disjunction N ∨ K still comes out true, so the third premise places no constraint on N.
Q610.L4f: The argument is invalid, and the counterexample is the case where L and M are true while K and N are false.

Q275.L1t: The least common multiple and greatest common divisor are both defined for any pair of integers.
Q275.L2t: The greatest common divisor of two integers divides each of them and also divides their least common multiple.
Q275.L3t: For two positive integers, the product of the numbers equals the product of their least common multiple and greatest common divisor, so dividing 240 times 24 by 48 gives the missing number.
Q275.L4t: The other integer is one hundred twenty.
Q275.L2f: The greatest common divisor of two integers is always a prime number.
Q275.L3f: Because 48 is already a multiple of the greatest common divisor, the other integer has to be the smallest positive integer, since the divisor already accounts for all shared factors.

Q320.L1t: Particles in circular motion can have both a tangential and a centripetal component of acceleration.
Q320.L2t: Centripetal acceleration points toward the center and is perpendicular to the velocity, while tangential acceleration points along the velocity.
Q320.L3t: The tangential acceleration is 10 m/s² and the centripetal acceleration v²/r is 100/10 = 10 m/s², so the two perpendicular components of acceleration are equal in size.
Q320.L4t: The velocity and acceleration vectors make an angle of forty-five degrees.
Q320.L2f: Tangential acceleration measures how quickly the direction of the velocity changes.
Q320.L3f: The centripetal acceleration here works out to about 17 m/s², roughly 1.7 times the tangential acceleration of 10 m/s².
Q320.L4f: The angle between the velocity and acceleration vectors is sixty degrees.

Q276.L1t: Successive percentage markdowns are a common setup in retail pricing problems.
Q276.L2t: The coat started at a list price of $325.00 and was marked down in two separate stages across November and December.
Q276.L3t: The December 10 percent markdown applies to the reduced November price, which is 80 percent of list, so the final price is the list price times 0.8 times 0.9.
Q276.L4t: The December shopper pays two hundred thirty-four dollars.
Q276.L2f: Retail markdowns are always calculated on the wholesale cost rather than on the list price.
Q276.L3f: Successive markdowns of 20 percent and 10 percent combine to a total discount of only about 11 percent off the list price.
Q276.L4f: The December shopper pays two hundred ninety dollars.

Q710.L1t: The minute hand of a clock turns 360 degrees every hour, while the hour hand turns 30 degrees every hour.
Q710.L2t: The minute hand moves 6 degrees per minute and the hour hand moves 0.5 degrees per minute, so the minute hand gains 5.5 degrees per minute on the hour hand.
Q710.L3t: Between 6 and 7 the angle between the hands is |180 - 5.5t| for t minutes past 6, so 110 degrees occurs at two times, t = 70/5.5 and t = 290/5.5, and the time away is the difference between them.
Q710.L4t: John was away for exactly 40 minutes.
Q710.L2f: On a standard clock the hour hand moves 1 degree per minute, and the minute hand moves 6 degrees per minute.
Q710.L3f: The two times when the hands are 110 degrees apart after 6 are about 13.4 minutes and 51.4 minutes past the hour, which are separated by 38 minutes.

Q649.L1t: Diffraction is the spreading of waves as they pass through an opening or around an obstacle, and it is strongest when the opening is comparable to the wavelength.
Q649.L2t: For a single slit of width a, dark minima occur at angles where a sin(theta) = m times the wavelength, with m = 1, 2, 3, and so on.
Q649.L3t: The first minimum at 45 degrees requires wavelength = 0.14 m times sin 45 degrees, which is about 0.099 m, and frequency equals the 350 m/s speed divided by that wavelength.
Q649.L4t: The first minimum at that angle falls at about 3,500 Hz.
Q649.L2f: Diffraction through a slit is negligible for sound, because audible wavelengths are always much smaller than a slit of this size.
Q649.L3f: The wavelength that produces the first minimum at 45 degrees works out to about 0.7 m, and dividing the 350 m/s speed by it gives the frequency.
Q649.L4f: The sound first disappears at the lowest frequency listed, about one-seventh of the highest frequency listed.

Q327.L1t: A cube has six faces, eight vertices, and twelve edges, and each vertex touches exactly three faces.
Q327.L2t: The number 1001 factors into the primes 7, 11, and 13.
Q327.L3t: Summing the eight vertex products gives (a+b)(c+d)(e+f), where each bracket is the sum of one pair of opposite faces, so 1001 must split into three integer factors each at least 2.
Q327.L4t: The three opposite-face sums are 7, 11, and 13, so the face numbers add up to 31.
Q327.L2f: Each face of the cube touches exactly four vertices, so each face number appears in four of the eight vertex products.
Q327.L3f: The total of the vertex products equals the sum of the faces multiplied together, so only the two smallest prime factors of 1001 matter and the face sum is 7 + 11.
Q327.L4f: The sum of the numbers on the faces is 18.

Q632.L1t: Superconductors are materials that conduct electricity with zero resistance below a critical temperature.
Q632.L2t: BCS theory, proposed in 1957 by Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer, explains conventional superconductivity through electrons forming bound Cooper pairs.
Q632.L3t: In the BCS mechanism, an electron distorts the lattice of positive ions as it passes, and a second electron is drawn toward that distortion, so phonons mediate the pairing.
Q632.L4t: The attraction between the paired electrons arises from their interaction with vibrations of the crystal's ionic lattice, exchanging phonons.
Q632.L2f: BCS theory was formulated in the 1920s, before quantum mechanics was developed, and describes Cooper pairs as bound states of an electron with a proton.
Q632.L3f: In BCS theory, the pairing arises because electrons polarize the vacuum around them, creating virtual particle-antiparticle pairs that screen their repulsion into a net attraction, independent of the crystal.
Q632.L4f: The attraction between Cooper pairs in BCS theory is due to vacuum polarization.

Q613.L1t: Total cost in a business setting combines a one-time startup expense with expenses that recur over time.
Q613.L2t: A one-time initial cost is a fixed amount, while operational and labor costs accumulate for each day the restaurant is open.
Q613.L3t: The daily costs of $250 and $400 are both paid each day, so they add to $650 per day, and this is multiplied by D days and added to the fixed $800,000.
Q613.L4t: The total cost is the $800,000 startup amount plus $650 for each of D days.
Q613.L2f: The initial cost is a one-time expense that is charged again each day, while daily costs are paid only once at opening.
Q613.L3f: The $800,000 initial cost is incurred again every day the restaurant is open, so it must be multiplied by the number of days, while the combined daily costs are paid just once.
Q613.L4f: The total cost is $650 plus $800,000 for each of D days.

Q292.L1t: Geometric probability compares the size of a favorable region to the size of the whole sample region.
Q292.L2t: The point is chosen uniformly from a cube with side length 2, and the condition x²+y²+z²≤1 describes a solid ball of radius 1 centered at the origin.
Q292.L3t: The probability equals the ball's volume (4/3)π(1)³ divided by the cube's volume 2³ = 8.
Q292.L4t: The probability is one sixth of pi.
Q292.L2f: The point is chosen uniformly from a cube with side length 2, and the condition x²+y²+z²≤1 describes a circle of radius 1 in the plane.
Q292.L3f: The cube has volume 8, but the ball's volume should be computed as (1/3)π r³ with r = 1, which gives a favorable volume of π/3 and a ratio of π/24 times 2.
Q292.L4f: The probability is pi over twelve.

Q701.L1t: Reflecting a graph across the y-axis replaces each x-coordinate with its opposite.
Q701.L2t: A function g defined by g(x) = f(–x) is the reflection of f across the y-axis.
Q701.L3t: Since g(3) = f(–3) and g(3) = 2, the point on f has x-coordinate –3 and the same y-value of 2.
Q701.L4t: The point (–3, 2) must lie on the graph of f.
Q701.L2f: Replacing x with –x in a function's rule reflects its graph across the x-axis, so y-values change sign.
Q701.L3f: Because g(x) = f(–x) has the same output at x as f does, g and f share the same input and output values at every point.
Q701.L4f: The point (3, 2) must be on the graph of f, because f and g pass through the same points.

Q324.L1t: Counting integers in a range depends on knowing exactly where the range starts and ends.
Q324.L2t: The three-digit positive integers run from 100 through 999, and all of them are included.
Q324.L3t: There are 999 positive integers up to 999, and the 99 numbers from 1 to 99 are not three-digit, so subtract them.
Q324.L4t: There are nine hundred three-digit positive integers.
Q324.L2f: The smallest three-digit positive integer is 101, because 100 is counted as a two-digit number.
Q324.L3f: The count of integers from 100 to 999 is found by subtracting 100 from 999 and not adding 1, since endpoints are not counted.
Q324.L4f: There are eight hundred ninety-nine three-digit positive integers.

Q306.L1t: The median of a data set is its middle value once the values are sorted, and for an even count it is the mean of the two middle values.
Q306.L2t: Sarah's five earlier times sorted are 86, 88, 94, 96 and 97, so her median before the sixth try was 94.
Q306.L3t: With six times the median is the mean of the third and fourth values, and for it to be 92 the new time must sit between 88 and 94 and pair with 94 to average 92.
Q306.L4t: Her sixth time was ninety seconds.
Q306.L2f: Sarah's five earlier times had a median of 96 seconds, since 96 is the middle number in the order she swam them.
Q306.L3f: Her sixth time must be a very short one, because bringing the median down requires a time far below all her previous times.
Q306.L4f: Her sixth time was only ten seconds.

Q302.L1t: Prime factorization expresses every integer greater than 1 as a product of primes, and a factor of a number is any integer that divides it evenly.
Q302.L2t: Whether a number must be divisible by a given integer depends on whether all of that integer's prime factors, with their multiplicities, are guaranteed to appear in the number.
Q302.L3t: The listed primes each appear at least once, but nothing says any prime is repeated, and a factor that needs a prime not on the list, or a repeated prime, cannot be guaranteed.
Q302.L4t: The number must be divisible by ten, because both of its prime factors, two and five, are guaranteed to appear in it.
Q302.L2f: A number whose prime factors are listed is always divisible by every prime on the list raised to the second power, since each prime must appear at least twice.
Q302.L3f: Since the number is even, its smallest prime factor must appear at least twice, so the number is always divisible by the square of that prime.
Q302.L4f: The number must be divisible by four.

Q637.L1t: The Doppler effect changes the observed frequency of a wave when the source or the observer moves relative to the medium carrying the wave.
Q637.L2t: An echo from a stationary wall involves two Doppler shifts: the wall acts as an observer of the moving source, then as a stationary source re-emitting the received frequency toward the moving driver.
Q637.L3t: The wall receives a frequency of 600 × 350/346.5, about 606 Hz, and then re-emits that frequency toward the driver, who is moving toward it, so the received frequency is multiplied again by 353.5/350.
Q637.L4t: After both shifts the driver hears the echo at about 612 Hz.
Q637.L2f: The Doppler shift for sound depends only on the ratio of the source speed to the speed of sound and does not depend on whether the observer is moving.
Q637.L3f: Only the shift at the wall matters, because the reflected sound travels back to the driver at the wall's received frequency, and the driver's own motion adds no further change.
Q637.L4f: The driver hears the echo at about 606 Hz.

Q663.L1t: Counting problems about random assignments of items to positions are solved by comparing the number of favorable arrangements with the total number of equally likely arrangements.
Q663.L2t: There are 4! = 24 equally likely ways to deliver four distinct packages to four houses, one per house, and a derangement is an arrangement in which no item is in its correct place.
Q663.L3t: Choosing which two houses get the right package can be done in 6 ways, and the other two packages must then both be wrong, which for just two items can happen in only one way (they are swapped).
Q663.L4t: Six of the 24 equally likely arrangements have exactly two correct deliveries, so the probability is one quarter.
Q663.L2f: Each package independently has a one-in-four chance of reaching its correct house, so the number of correct deliveries follows a binomial distribution with four trials.
Q663.L3f: Because each of the four packages independently lands at the right house with probability one fourth, the chance that exactly two do is 6 × (1/4)² × (3/4)².
Q663.L4f: The probability is twenty-seven over one hundred twenty-eight.

Q304.L1t: Two lines in the coordinate plane are perpendicular when they meet at a right angle.
Q304.L2t: The line x + 2y + 3 = 0 can be rewritten in slope-intercept form with a y-intercept of -3/2.
Q304.L3t: The two lines have slopes -1/2 and -a/2, and perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is -1.
Q304.L4t: The value of a is negative four.
Q304.L2f: The line x + 2y + 3 = 0 crosses the y-axis at the point where y equals positive 3/2.
Q304.L3f: Two lines of this form are perpendicular exactly when the coefficient of x in the second equation plus 4 equals -11.
Q304.L4f: The value of a is negative fifteen.

Q723.L1t: Propositional logic uses capital letters for simple sentences and combines them with connectives such as conjunction, disjunction and negation.
Q723.L2t: In PL, the word 'but' is normally symbolized with the same connective as 'and'.
Q723.L3t: Conjunction is a binary connective, so joining three components requires parentheses to group two of them first and give a well-formed formula.
Q723.L4t: The best symbolization groups the fish-and-lizards conjunction together, then conjoins that with the negation of cats.
Q723.L2f: In PL, the tilde is a binary connective that must be placed between two sentence letters.
Q723.L3f: PL lets any number of conjuncts be strung together with no parentheses, because grouping is never needed for conjunction.
Q723.L4f: The best symbolization is the ungrouped three-way conjunction of the fish letter, the lizard letter and the negated cat letter.

Q629.L1t: Identities for squaring a binomial are commonly used to simplify algebraic expressions.
Q629.L2t: The identity (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 applies to the squared expression given in the problem.
Q629.L3t: Expanding the given square yields 4x^2 + 12xy + 9y^2 = 4, so the target expression equals 4 minus 12xy, and xy is known.
Q629.L2f: For any real numbers a and b, the square of (a + b) is always equal to a^2 + b^2.
Q629.L3f: The cross term drops out here, so 4x^2 + 9y^2 is simply the sum of the coefficients of the squared terms.
Q629.L4f: The value of the expression is thirteen.

Q282.L1t: Exponential growth and decay models describe quantities whose rate of change is proportional to the current amount.
Q282.L2t: A quantity whose rate of change is proportional to its size obeys dP/dt = kP, whose solutions have the form P = P0·e^(kt).
Q282.L3t: Because the growth is exponential, the population is 200·3^(t/10), and one full day of 24 hours puts the exponent at 2.4.
Q282.L4t: After a full day the population is about 2793 bacteria.
Q282.L2f: In a growth model where the rate is proportional to the population, the doubling time shrinks steadily as the culture gets larger.
Q282.L3f: Because the population adds a fixed number of bacteria each hour, tripling in ten hours means a gain of 40 per hour over the full day.
Q282.L4f: After a full day the population is about 1160 bacteria.

Q325.L1t: Predicate logic uses quantifiers and predicates to express the logical form of English statements.
Q325.L2t: A universal claim about members of a category is normally translated with a universal quantifier whose scope is a conditional rather than a conjunction.
Q325.L3t: The statement says that for anything, if it is a planet then it is smaller than Jupiter, and since Sxy means x is smaller than y, the planet goes in the first place and Jupiter in the second.
Q325.L4t: The correct translation says that for every x, if x is a planet then x is smaller than Jupiter.
Q325.L2f: In predicate logic a universal claim about a category is normally translated with an existential quantifier joined to a conjunction.
Q325.L3f: In the predicate Sxy the larger object goes first, so Jupiter must take the first place in the relation and the planet the second.
Q325.L4f: The correct translation says that for every x, if x is a planet then Jupiter is smaller than x.

Q310.L1t: A regular octagon is a polygon with eight equal sides and eight equal interior angles.
Q310.L2t: A diagonal is a segment joining two vertices of a polygon that are not next to each other.
Q310.L3t: Each of the 8 vertices connects by a diagonal to the 5 vertices that are neither itself nor its two neighbours, and every diagonal is counted twice that way.
Q310.L4t: A regular octagon has twenty diagonals.
Q310.L2f: In any convex polygon the number of diagonals is always equal to the number of sides.
Q310.L3f: Each vertex of an octagon has exactly two diagonals, and since each diagonal has only one starting vertex, no halving is needed.
Q310.L4f: A regular octagon has sixteen diagonals.

Q690.L1t: Predicate logic uses quantifiers and a translation key to turn English sentences into symbolic form.
Q690.L2t: In this formula the existential quantifier sits inside the consequent of the conditional, and the universal quantifier governs the whole conditional.
Q690.L3t: The outer universal quantifier ranges over apartments, and for each apartment the consequent only requires at least one house that it exceeds in size.
Q690.L4t: The formula says that each apartment is larger than at least one house.
Q690.L2f: In a translation key, a two-place predicate like Bxy is always read with the second variable as the larger item.
Q690.L3f: The formula's universal quantifier effectively ranges over houses, and the comparison must hold against every apartment without exception.
Q690.L4f: The formula says that every house is larger than all of the apartments.

Q718.L1t: Percentage increases are commonly used to work out how a salary grows over several years.
Q718.L2t: Percentage raises compound, so each year's raise is based on the salary at the start of that year.
Q718.L3t: The first raise brings the salary to $22,000, and the second raise is 10% of that new amount, which is $2,200.
Q718.L4t: After two years her salary would be twenty-four thousand two hundred dollars.
Q718.L2f: A ten percent increase is found by multiplying the salary by 0.10 and then subtracting that figure from it.
Q718.L3f: Only one raise changes her pay, because the second increase is already counted inside the first.
Q718.L4f: After the two years her salary would be twenty-two thousand dollars.

Q603.L1t: Regular polygons have equal sides and equal angles, and their angle measures follow from the number of sides.
Q603.L2t: A regular octagon has eight congruent sides and eight congruent interior angles.
Q603.L3t: The interior angles of an eight-sided polygon sum to 6 times 180 degrees, which is 1080 degrees, and a regular one shares that total equally among its eight angles.
Q603.L4t: Each interior angle of the sign measures one hundred thirty-five degrees.
Q603.L2f: A regular octagon has sides of unequal lengths but all of its angles are equal.
Q603.L3f: Every regular polygon with four or more sides has corners that are right angles, so the sign's interior angle is a quarter turn.
Q603.L4f: Each interior angle of the sign is a right angle, measuring ninety degrees.

Q715.L1t: Word problems about fractions of a quantity are usually solved by turning the wording into an equation.
Q715.L2t: One-half of one-third of a pile is one-sixth of that pile, and the two piles were equal in size.
Q715.L3t: The brother's gift is one-sixth of a single pile, so John's remainder is the whole of both piles minus that one-sixth, which equals eleven-sixths of one pile.
Q715.L2f: Taking one-half of one-third of a quantity removes exactly one-fourth of it.
Q715.L3f: The 66 pins John had left equal one-sixth of his original total, so the total is six times the amount left.
Q715.L4f: John originally had three hundred ninety-six pins.

Q662.L1t: Geometric probability problems on a circle often reduce to comparing arc lengths with the full circumference.
Q662.L2t: A chord's length depends on the central angle it subtends, and chord length grows as that angle grows from 0 to 180 degrees.
Q662.L3t: A chord is shorter than the radius exactly when its central angle is under 60 degrees, so all three points must lie within a common arc of one-sixth of the circle.
Q662.L4t: The probability is one in twelve.
Q662.L2f: The chord length between two points on a circle depends only on the radius and not on how far apart the points are.
Q662.L3f: A chord equals the radius when its central angle is 45 degrees, so all three points must fit within an eighth of the circle and the favorable count is 2 times the square of one-eighth.
Q662.L4f: The probability is one in thirty-two.

Q729.L1t: Coordinate geometry lets you compute lengths and areas of polygons directly from vertex coordinates.
Q729.L2t: Opposite vertices of a square are the endpoints of a diagonal, and the distance formula gives the length between any two coordinate points.
Q729.L3t: The area of a square equals half the square of its diagonal, and here the diagonal's squared length is 6 squared plus 2 squared.
Q729.L4t: The square has an area of twenty.
Q729.L2f: The two diagonals of a square are perpendicular but have different lengths.
Q729.L3f: The side of the square runs between the two given points with legs of 3 and 5, so the side squared is the sum of those squares and the area follows directly.
Q729.L4f: The square has an area of thirty-four.

Q631.L1t: Positronium is a bound state of an electron and its antiparticle, the positron.
Q631.L2t: Positronium has hydrogen-like Bohr energy levels, but they are scaled by the system's reduced mass, which differs from hydrogen's.
Q631.L3t: The electron-positron reduced mass is half the electron mass, so the levels are half of hydrogen's, -13.6/(2n²) eV, and the n=3 to n=1 gap is that ground-state value times (1 - 1/9).
Q631.L4t: The emitted photon has an energy of about 6.0 eV.
Q631.L2f: Positronium is a perfectly stable atom that never decays, because the electron and positron cannot annihilate each other.
Q631.L3f: The n=3 level lies essentially at the ionization threshold, so the transition releases the whole ground-state binding energy of positronium, which is half of hydrogen's.
Q631.L4f: The photon carries the full positronium ground-state binding energy, half of hydrogen's 13.6 eV, so that is the correct answer.

Q722.L1t: An indirect truth table tests consistency by assuming every proposition in the set is true and looking for a contradiction.
Q722.L2t: The third proposition is a conjunction, so it can be true only if both of its conjuncts are true.
Q722.L3t: The third proposition makes N true and Q false. With Q false, the conditional needs ~O to be false, so O is true. With N true, the biconditional's left side is false, so O·P must be false, which forces P to be false.
Q722.L4t: The set is consistent, and a valuation that makes all three true has N and O true and P and Q false.
Q722.L2f: A conjunction is true whenever at least one of its conjuncts is true.
Q722.L3f: With Q false, the conditional ~O ⊃ Q can hold only if O is false, yet N being true makes the biconditional require O·P to be true, so the required values clash.
Q722.L4f: No assignment of truth values makes all three propositions true at once, so the set is inconsistent.

Q625.L1t: Translating PL formulas into English requires a key that matches each sentence letter to a simple English sentence.
Q625.L2t: In this key C stands for Emily stopping work and D for Russell making dinner, and in the formula the tilde attaches only to C.
Q625.L3t: The formula is a disjunction whose first disjunct is the negation of C, and 'unless' is the English form of a disjunction, so the translation must say Emily does not stop working, not leave that part affirmative.
Q625.L4t: The formula is rendered as 'Emily doesn't stop working unless Russell makes dinner.'
Q625.L2f: In this key the letter D stands for Ashleigh stopping by.
Q625.L3f: The tilde is absorbed into the 'unless' construction and drops out in translation, so the formula says the same thing as a plain disjunction of C with D.
Q625.L4f: The formula says Emily stops working, with no negation, unless Russell makes dinner, so that unnegated 'unless' sentence is the correct translation.

Q650.L1t: Completing the square rewrites a quadratic into vertex form, which shows its maximum or minimum value and where it occurs.
Q650.L2t: The leading coefficient of -2 must be factored out of the x-squared and x terms before completing the square, and it then multiplies whatever is added inside the parentheses.
Q650.L3t: Factoring gives -2(x^2+10x)-53, and adding 25 inside the parentheses means 50 is added to the expression, so the constant must be adjusted by subtracting 50 again, leaving -3 once combined with -53.
Q650.L4t: The vertex form is -2(x+5)^2-3, so the constants add up to zero.
Q650.L2f: Completing the square on a quadratic with a leading coefficient other than 1 requires dividing the whole expression by that coefficient, which changes the value of the constants.
Q650.L3f: After factoring out -2 and completing the square, the 25 added inside the parentheses adds 25 to the expression, not 50, so the constant becomes -53+25 with its sign flipped to positive 3 once rewritten.
Q650.L4f: The three constants a, d and e add up to a small positive number, six, not zero.

Q683.L1t: Order of operations means multiplication is carried out before addition and subtraction when no parentheses are used.
Q683.L2t: With the numbers fixed in order as 2, 4, 6, 8 and each symbol used exactly once, there are only six possible arrangements to compare.
Q683.L3t: Multiplication gives the most when it joins the two largest adjacent numbers, 6 and 8, giving 48, and the best use of the remaining symbols is to subtract the 4 from the 2 rather than add it, since 2-4 costs only 2 whereas the alternative arrangements waste the multiplication on smaller numbers.
Q683.L4t: The best arrangement is 2-4+6×8, which gives forty-six.
Q683.L2f: When no parentheses are given, the symbols are evaluated strictly from left to right, so the multiplication has no special priority over the addition or subtraction.
Q683.L3f: The highest total comes from doing the additions first and then using multiplication last so that it scales the whole accumulated sum, because multiplying a larger sum always beats multiplying only the last two numbers.
Q683.L4f: The highest possible result is the larger of the two upper choices, the value just below one hundred.

Q635.L1t: A percent increase compares how much larger one quantity is than another, measured against a chosen base quantity.
Q635.L2t: The square root of 121 is exactly 11, while the square root of 200 is not a whole number and lies between 14 and 15.
Q635.L3t: The percent larger is the difference between the two roots divided by the smaller root, so it equals about 3.14 divided by 11, and this ratio is a little over a quarter.
Q635.L4t: The larger root is about 28.6 percent bigger, which rounds to twenty-nine.
Q635.L2f: The square root of 200 is a whole number just above fourteen, so the comparison between the two roots can be done exactly without any rounding.
Q635.L3f: A percent larger depends only on the smaller root's own whole-number value, since the difference between the roots cancels out when the ratio is formed.
Q635.L4f: The percent by which the larger root exceeds the smaller one equals the whole-number value of the smaller root itself.

Q654.L1t: Propositional logic symbolization turns English sentences into formulas using letters for simple statements and connectives such as conjunction, disjunction and the conditional.
Q654.L2t: In this sentence the letters stand for the person having lived with you for the year (L), being born in the year (B), dying in the year (D), and your home having been the person's home for their whole life (H).
Q654.L3t: The phrase 'is considered to have lived with you if' makes the stated conditions the antecedent and 'lived with you' the consequent, and the conditions are that the person was born or died and the home requirement also held.
Q654.L4t: The best symbolization is a conditional whose antecedent is the conjunction of 'born or died' with 'home was this person's home', and whose consequent is that the person lived with you.
Q654.L2f: In symbolization, the English word 'if' is conventionally rendered as a biconditional, so the sentence's two sides are treated as logically equivalent.

Q717.L1t: Arithmetic and geometric progressions are sequences defined by a constant difference or a constant ratio between consecutive terms.
Q717.L2t: An arithmetic progression starting at 9 can be written as 9, 9+d, 9+2d, where d is the common difference.
Q717.L3t: After the additions the terms are 9, 11+d and 29+2d, and the geometric condition (11+d)² = 9(29+2d) reduces to d² + 4d − 140 = 0, which has two real roots whose third-term values 29+2d can be compared.
Q717.L4t: The smaller of the two possible third terms of the geometric progression is one.
Q717.L2f: In a geometric progression the difference between consecutive terms must be constant, so the middle term equals the average of its neighbours.
Q717.L3f: Solving the geometric condition shows that the common difference of the original progression must be −6.5, the only admissible value.
Q717.L4f: The smallest possible third term of the geometric progression is sixteen.

Q659.L1t: A moving charge in combined electric and magnetic fields feels the Lorentz force, the sum of an electric force and a magnetic force.
Q659.L2t: A proton accelerated from rest through a potential difference V gains kinetic energy qV, so its speed grows with the square root of V.
Q659.L3t: At the original speed the electric force along +x balances the magnetic force qv×B, which for velocity along +z and field along +y points along −x, and since only the magnetic force depends on speed, a faster proton gets a larger magnetic force than electric force.
Q659.L4t: With the doubled potential difference the proton moves faster, the magnetic force wins, and the proton is deflected toward the negative x-direction.

Q659.L3f: The magnetic force on the proton points along the direction of the magnetic field, so a faster proton feels a larger push along +y.
Q659.L4f: With the doubled potential difference the proton moves faster and is deflected in the positive y-direction, along the magnetic field.

Q656.L1t: A truth table lists every combination of truth values for the sentence letters, and an argument is valid only if no row makes all premises true and the conclusion false.
Q656.L2t: A biconditional is true exactly when its two sides have the same truth value, so a negated biconditional is true exactly when the two sides differ.

Q656.L4t: No row makes both premises true while N is false, so the argument is valid and has no counterexample.

Q656.L3f: The first premise comes out true in the row where N is true and M is false, and the premise M can be set aside when checking that row.
Q656.L4f: The argument is invalid, because the row with N true and M false makes the premises true while the conclusion fails.

Q698.L1t: A multiple of a number is the product of that number and an integer, and every integer has infinitely many multiples.
Q698.L2t: To say 12 is a multiple of an integer is the same as saying that integer divides 12 evenly, so the question is really about counting the divisors of 12.
Q698.L3t: The positive divisors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, and each has a negative counterpart that also divides 12, so the total is twice the positive count.
Q698.L4t: Counting both signs, 12 is a multiple of twelve integers.
Q698.L2f: A number is a multiple of only those integers that are smaller than it, since a larger integer can never divide it evenly.
Q698.L3f: Only the positive divisors count here, and they are limited to the proper factor pairs of 12 that remain after excluding 1 and 12.
Q698.L4f: The right count is the number of positive factors that are neither the smallest nor the largest, taken once, so the answer is the smaller of the two middle values.

Q604.L1t: A parametric curve gives x and y as functions of a parameter t, and its slope is found by dividing dy/dt by dx/dt.
Q604.L2t: For this curve dx/dt equals 2t and dy/dt equals 2^t times ln 2, so the slope at a given t is 2^t ln 2 divided by 2t.
Q604.L3t: Setting 2^t equal to 4 gives t = 2, and substituting that t into both x = t^2 + 1 and the slope formula gives the point and the slope to use.
Q604.L4t: The tangent passes through the point with x equal to 5 and y equal to 4, and its slope is ln 2.
Q604.L2f: The derivative of 2^t with respect to t is t times 2^(t-1), so the exponential differentiates like a power function.
Q604.L3f: The x-coordinate of the tangent point is the parameter value itself, so t = 2 is used directly as the x-value in the point-slope form.
Q604.L4f: The tangent line is the one through the point where x equals 2, with slope ln 2.

Q700.L1t: Standing waves in pipes form at frequencies set by the pipe's length and the speed of sound in the air inside it.
Q700.L2t: An open pipe has an antinode of displacement at each end, so it supports every integer multiple of its fundamental frequency.
Q700.L3t: A pipe closed at one end has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so its fundamental is half the open pipe's, 25 Hz, and only odd multiples of that appear (25, 75, 125, 175, 225 Hz and so on).
Q700.L4t: Once the pipe is closed at one end, none of the original five frequencies is still present.
Q700.L2f: An open pipe supports only the odd-numbered harmonics, because both of its ends must be displacement nodes.
Q700.L3f: Closing one end keeps the open pipe's own frequencies but removes the fundamental and every even-numbered harmonic, leaving the higher odd ones.
Q700.L4f: After closing one end, the higher odd harmonics, 150 Hz and 250 Hz, are the ones that remain.

Q675.L1t: A pair of linear equations in two unknowns can be solved by elimination or by substitution.
Q675.L2t: The coefficients of the two equations are not proportional, so the system has exactly one solution for x and y.
Q675.L3t: Subtracting the first equation from the second gives x + y = 2, and substituting that into the first equation leaves 2y = 50, so y and then x can be found.

Q675.L2f: The two equations are multiples of each other, so the system has infinitely many solutions.

Q675.L4f: The value of x - y is positive two.

Q652.L1t: An argument is valid only if no assignment of truth values makes every premise true and the conclusion false.
Q652.L2t: An indirect truth table assumes the premises are true and the conclusion false, then checks whether those assumptions can be held consistently.
Q652.L3t: For the conclusion to be false, L and R must be true and P false; the third premise then forces Q false, which makes the consequent of the second premise false, so N must be true and O false to keep that premise true.
Q652.L4t: The argument is invalid, because the premises can all be true while the conclusion is false.
Q652.L2f: An indirect truth table shows an argument is invalid when assuming true premises and a true conclusion produces consistent values.
Q652.L3f: When L and R are true and P is false, the third premise forces Q to be true, which makes the second premise's consequent true and so blocks any way of falsifying the conclusion.
Q652.L4f: The argument is valid, because no assignment makes all the premises true and the conclusion false.

Q687.L1t: An indirect truth table tests consistency by assuming every proposition in the set is true and checking whether any assignment of truth values makes that possible.
Q687.L2t: A conditional with a false antecedent is true, so the second proposition is satisfied automatically whenever T is false.
Q687.L3t: If T is false, then T ⊃ U is true, so the first proposition holds only when W ⊃ U also holds, which means W being true forces U to be true.
Q687.L4t: The set is consistent, and making U, W and X true and T false gives all three propositions the value true.
Q687.L2f: A set of propositions counts as consistent only if all of its members are true under every possible valuation.
Q687.L3f: If T is false, the consequent W ⊃ U of the first proposition is true whatever values W and U take.
Q687.L4f: The set is consistent, and making W and X true and T and U false is a valuation that makes all three propositions true.

Q616.L1t: In predicate logic, universal claims are normally translated with a universal quantifier over a conditional, and existential claims with a conjunction.
Q616.L2t: A statement of the form 'No S are G' is a universal negative, which can be written as a universal conditional with a negated consequent or as the negation of an existential claim.
Q616.L3t: Reading G as 'graduates without a major', the sentence says that anything that is a senior is not such a graduate, so 'senior' belongs in the antecedent.
Q616.L4t: The sentence is a universal negative: for every individual, being a senior implies not being someone who graduates without a major.
Q616.L2f: Universal negative statements such as 'No S are G' are standardly formalized with an existential quantifier governing a conditional.
Q616.L3f: The word 'no' negates the subject term, so the antecedent of the conditional should be the negation of 'senior'.
Q616.L4f: The best translation says that every individual who is not a senior fails to graduate, which makes seniors the only people who can graduate.

Q608.L1t: Symbolizing an English sentence in propositional logic means picking out the atomic claims, assigning each a letter, and working out how connectives like 'either...or' and 'if...then' join them.
Q608.L2t: The phrases 'sufficient condition' and 'necessary condition' map onto opposite directions of the conditional, so confusing them reverses the antecedent and consequent.
Q608.L3t: To say that one claim is a sufficient condition for another is to say that its truth guarantees the other's, so the sufficient claim is the antecedent and the other is the consequent.
Q608.L4t: The first disjunct has England's importing beef as antecedent and France's subsidizing agriculture as consequent, while the second has South Africa's supplying diamonds as antecedent and China's promoting human rights as consequent.
Q608.L2f: An 'either...or' sentence whose parts are themselves conditionals is always symbolized in propositional logic with a conjunction rather than a disjunction.
Q608.L3f: A sufficient condition is what the other claim requires, so it goes in the consequent: 'p is sufficient for q' is written as q ⊃ p.
Q608.L4f: The first disjunct should have France's subsidizing agriculture as antecedent and England's importing beef as consequent, with the second disjunct having South Africa's supplying diamonds as antecedent, so that is the correct symbolization.

Q810.L1t: The passage is a program recap about how clothing styles and fashion changed in China over thirty years of reform and opening-up.

Q865.L1t: The passage is a nature news report about butterflies and wildlife conservation in Britain.

Q865.L3t: The text opens with a sighting of a butterfly in Britain for the first time in sixty years, and the rest of the text builds on that single event, so the central point is that event rather than a habit of the insects.
Q865.L4t: The main idea is that a rare butterfly has turned up in Britain for the first time in decades.

Q865.L3f: The text mainly explains that butterflies deliberately migrate long distances every year as a regular habit, and the sighting is only an example of that habit.

Q776.L1t: The passage is a news-style obituary describing the long marriage, family life and community work of Helen and Kenneth Felumlee.

Q776.L3f: Working as an inspector and as a mechanic on the railroad was a single job, and teaching Sunday school was unpaid church volunteering, so only the railroad work and the mail carrier post count as his jobs.

Q813.L1t: The passage is a travel-style guide to several converted-factory art districts in Chinese cities, giving their addresses and opening hours.

Q813.L3t: The passage dates the start of each art district: Guangzhou in 2009, Chongqing in the early 2000s, and Shanghai with its first studio in 2002, whereas artists began moving into the Beijing factory buildings in 2001.

Q838.L1t: The passage is an essay about medical ethics and honesty in professional practice.
Q838.L2t: The passage notes that other professions, such as law and government, also face situations where deception seems to avoid serious consequences.
Q838.L3t: The passage opens by asking whether doctors should ever lie to patients, uses a cancer patient as its example, and then argues that truthful information helps patients cope, so it urges open debate over the doctor's choice between telling and hiding the truth.
Q838.L4t: The passage is mainly about whether doctors should tell patients the truth about their illness.

Q838.L4f: The passage is mainly about whether more studies should be carried out on this subject.

Q762.L1t: The passage is a first-person account of a teenager who takes pride in being a good big brother to his younger siblings.
Q762.L2t: The author's brother was hit by a pick-up truck at age nine and has used a wheelchair for six years.
Q762.L3t: The author says he watches over four sisters and a brother besides himself, which makes six children, and a family like this would very probably also include two parents.
