Q851.L1t: The Spring Festival is China's most important traditional holiday, a time for family reunions and festive customs.
Q851.L2t: Chinese New Year's Day is calculated by the Chinese lunar calendar, and in 2015 it fell on February 19.
Q851.L3t: The celebrations traditionally begin on the 23rd day of the 12th lunar month and end on the 15th day of the first lunar month, and a lunar month lasts about 29 to 30 days.
Q851.L4t: Traditionally the festival lasts about twenty-three days, from the 23rd of the twelfth lunar month to the 15th of the first.
Q851.L2f: Chinese New Year's Day is calculated by the solar Gregorian calendar and falls on the same date every year.
Q851.L3f: The traditional festival is defined by the national holiday, which runs from the Eve to the seventh day of the first lunar month, with no celebrations before or after.
Q851.L4f: Traditionally the festival lasts only about one week, ending when offices and schools reopen after the seventh day of the first lunar month.

Q961.L1t: Tort law decides when a person who injures another through careless or wrongful conduct must pay damages.
Q961.L2t: Violating a safety statute can amount to negligence per se, but courts recognize certain excuses for the violation.
Q961.L3t: An emergency not of the actor's own making excuses a statutory violation if the actor behaves reasonably, and here the car went out of control despite the husband's reasonable efforts while he rushed his child, who had stopped breathing, to the hospital.
Q961.L4t: The driver will not recover, because the husband acted reasonably in a genuine emergency, which excuses his crossing of the center line.
Q961.L2f: Negligence per se arises only when the statute expressly creates a private right to sue for damages.
Q961.L3f: Once the husband's car crossed the line, the oncoming driver had a final opportunity to avoid the collision, and that doctrine bars recovery regardless of the husband's emergency.
Q961.L4f: The driver's claim fails because the driver had a final opportunity to avoid the crash and did not take it.

Q901.L1t: Under agency and tort law, a business can sometimes be held responsible for harm caused by another party who works on its behalf.
Q901.L2t: The manufacturer supplied nondefective materials, and the installer was a franchisee rather than an employee, so ordinary respondeat superior liability for employees does not apply.
Q901.L3t: The manufacturer knew its logo appeared on the installer's truck and literature, which led the homeowner to reasonably believe the installer was acting for the manufacturer, and a principal who allows such an appearance can be bound as though an agency existed.
Q901.L4t: The manufacturer can be held liable because it let the installer appear to be its agent, so the homeowner has a claim based on apparent agency.
Q901.L2f: A franchise agreement always gives the franchisor full day-to-day control over how the franchisee performs each job, though courts treat that control as irrelevant to liability.
Q901.L3f: The mere existence of a franchise relationship automatically makes the franchisor vicariously liable for the franchisee's negligence, regardless of what the customer saw or believed.
Q901.L4f: The homeowner has a claim against the manufacturer simply because the installer was its franchisee, whether or not any appearance of agency existed.

Q983.L1t: Graves disease is a common cause of thyrotoxicosis and is one of the main autoimmune disorders of the thyroid gland.
Q983.L2t: Graves disease is caused by autoantibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor, producing excess thyroid hormone and usually a diffusely enlarged gland.
Q983.L3t: Graves disease can involve the tissues behind the eye, where autoimmune inflammation and swelling of the extraocular muscles can restrict their movement.
Q983.L4t: Graves disease can cause paralysis or restriction of the eye muscles, which is known as ophthalmoplegia.
Q983.L2f: Graves disease is caused by destruction of thyroid tissue from chronic infection, which leads to underproduction of thyroid hormone.
Q983.L3f: In Graves disease the thyroid enlarges through the growth of many separate autonomously functioning nodules, which is the characteristic finding on examination.
Q983.L4f: Graves disease is characterised by a large multi-nodular goitre, so that is the correct statement.

Q391.L1t: Fatty acids are an important energy source that is stored in adipose tissue as triglycerides and released when the body needs fuel.
Q391.L2t: Free fatty acids are released from adipose tissue by hormone-sensitive lipase during fasting and exercise, and they are carried to tissues such as muscle and heart for oxidation.
Q391.L3t: Free fatty acids are poorly soluble in water, so in plasma they attach noncovalently to the most abundant plasma protein, which is made in the liver.
Q391.L4t: Most free fatty acids travel in the blood attached to the plasma protein albumin.
Q391.L2f: Free fatty acids are released from adipose tissue only after meals, when high insulin levels stimulate triglyceride breakdown.
Q391.L3f: Because free fatty acids need to be shielded from the plasma, they are mostly taken up and carried inside circulating blood cells that deliver them to tissues.
Q391.L4f: Most free fatty acids are carried in the blood inside the red blood cells, so that is the correct answer.

Q888.L1t: Neurological observation charts are used in hospitals to monitor patients with suspected or confirmed brain injury or neurological illness.
Q888.L2t: These charts typically record the Glasgow Coma Scale components, pupil size and reaction, limb movements and vital signs such as pulse and blood pressure.
Q888.L3t: Vital signs are a routine part of neurological observation charts, and body temperature is one of the standard vital signs recorded alongside the neurological assessments.
Q888.L4t: Temperature is a parameter that is typically recorded on neurological observation charts.
Q888.L2f: Neurological observation charts were first introduced in the 1990s as a replacement for the Glasgow Coma Scale and are completed only once a day.
Q888.L3f: Neurological observation charts are built around fluid balance monitoring, so the volume of urine passed is a standard recorded item on them.
Q888.L4f: Urine output is the parameter typically seen on neurological observation charts.

Q988.L1t: Strict liability in tort generally applies to defendants who place defective or unreasonably dangerous products into the stream of commerce.
Q988.L2t: Strict liability does not depend on fault, so a defendant's exercise of due care is generally not a defense in a strict liability action.
Q988.L3t: Strict liability attaches to those engaged in the business of selling products, and courts often treat a pharmacist's filling of a prescription as providing a professional service rather than the sale of a product.
Q988.L4t: The pharmacist's best defense is that he was not a seller of the product on whom strict liability may be imposed.
Q988.L2f: Strict liability in tort was created to hold only manufacturers liable and has never been applied to anyone else in the chain of distribution.
Q988.L3f: Under strict liability, only the person who personally receives payment from the customer counts as the seller, so a pharmacist who does not handle the money falls outside liability.
Q988.L4f: The pharmacist's best defense is that the cashier, and not he, personally received the money for the medication.

Q414.L1t: Drug doses are commonly calculated from a patient's body weight using a dose in milligrams per kilogram.
Q414.L2t: The dose in milligrams is found by multiplying the patient's weight in kilograms by the dose per kilogram, here 62 times 15.
Q414.L3t: The product 62 times 15 equals 930 mg, and since one gram is 1000 mg, that amount must be divided by 1000 to convert it to grams.
Q414.L4t: The dose is 0.93 grams, which is less than one gram.
Q414.L2f: Dosing by body weight is only used for adults, and the dose per kilogram is always given in grams rather than milligrams.
Q414.L3f: To convert 930 mg to grams you divide by 100, because one gram is equal to 100 mg.

Q956.L1t: The attorney-client privilege is a rule of evidence that protects some confidential communications between lawyers and those who consult them.
Q956.L2t: The attorney-client privilege can cover preliminary consultations with a prospective client, even when the lawyer is never retained for the case.
Q956.L3t: A parent who accompanies a child to a consultation is present as the client's agent, so their presence does not destroy confidentiality, and the privilege belongs to the child and is not waived by the child filing suit.
Q956.L4t: The attorney's testimony is inadmissible because the boy's statements were confidential communications made in a consultation with a prospective lawyer, so the attorney-client privilege bars the testimony.
Q956.L2f: The privilege for statements made to an attorney is lost for any consultation that does not end with the lawyer being formally retained and paid.
Q956.L3f: The only hearsay exception that could apply here covers statements about physical condition, and it applies only to statements made to a doctor in order to get medical treatment, with no protection from privilege for any other statement.
Q956.L4f: The attorney's testimony is inadmissible because the boy's statement about his physical condition was not made to obtain medical treatment, so it does not qualify for the hearsay exception.

Q930.L1t: Gene expression in cells involves two main stages, transcription and translation, which together turn the information in DNA into protein.
Q930.L2t: Translation takes place in the cytoplasm, where the nucleotide sequence of a messenger RNA is read in codons of three bases to build a chain of amino acids.
Q930.L3t: Translation is the step in which a ribosome reads the mRNA codons while tRNA molecules bring the matching amino acids, whereas DNA and RNA polymerase act earlier, in transcription.
Q930.L4t: Translation requires messenger RNA, transfer RNA and ribosomes working together to build the protein.
Q930.L2f: Translation takes place inside the nucleus, where the mRNA is read directly off the chromosomes as the protein is assembled.
Q930.L3f: RNA polymerase reads the DNA template and joins the amino acids into the polypeptide during translation, so both DNA and RNA polymerase must be present for protein synthesis to proceed.
Q930.L4f: Translation requires DNA, mRNA and RNA polymerase, because the enzyme reads the DNA to make the protein.

Q971.L1t: Recognising the early warning signs of serious medical problems lets first aiders and clinicians respond quickly and call for help.
Q971.L2t: Respiratory failure occurs when the lungs cannot take in enough oxygen or remove enough carbon dioxide from the blood.
Q971.L3t: When breathing fails, oxygen falls and carbon dioxide builds up in the blood, which depresses brain function and leads to tiredness, confusion and a falling level of responsiveness.
Q971.L4t: Exhaustion, confusion and unresponsiveness can be indicators of respiratory failure.
Q971.L2f: Being generally unwell is a specific clinical diagnosis with a defined set of signs that doctors test for, and it is a leading cause of hospital admission.
Q971.L3f: Exhaustion, confusion and unresponsiveness are vague, non-specific signs that appear with any minor illness and do not point to a particular organ system, so they just reflect a person who is run down.
Q971.L4f: Exhaustion, confusion and unresponsiveness are indicators of being generally unwell.

Q1001.L1t: Landlord-tenant law governs the rights and duties of the parties to a lease of residential property.
Q1001.L2t: A month-to-month tenancy is a periodic tenancy that continues from period to period until one party gives proper notice of termination.
Q1001.L3t: Many jurisdictions bar a landlord from ending a tenancy because the tenant successfully raised a habitability defense, and a notice given right after that defense succeeded is treated as retaliation even if its form is otherwise adequate.
Q1001.L4t: The tenant most likely won because the landlord's termination notice was a retaliatory response to the tenant's successful habitability defense in the earlier suit.
Q1001.L2f: A month-to-month tenancy can be created only by a signed lease that has been recorded with the county.
Q1001.L3f: Under the governing rule, ending any periodic tenancy requires notice of half a year, whatever the rental interval.
Q1001.L4f: The tenant won because the notice gave too little time, since half a year's notice was needed to end this tenancy.

Q1008.L1t: Tort law gives remedies for intentional and negligent interference with a person's emotional well-being.
Q1008.L2t: Intentional infliction of emotional distress requires extreme and outrageous conduct that intentionally or recklessly causes severe emotional distress.
Q1008.L3t: When a defendant commits outrageous conduct knowing a particular bystander is present, his recklessness toward that bystander is established, and the bystander can recover for harm his own vulnerability makes worse.
Q1008.L4t: The barber should recover, because the guard's awareness that the barber was in the shop supplies the intent or recklessness needed as to him.
Q1008.L2f: Intentional infliction of emotional distress is a strict liability tort that requires no showing of fault by the defendant.
Q1008.L3f: A defendant is never liable for distress consequences that a reasonable person could not have anticipated, and an unusual heart reaction falls outside that scope.
Q1008.L4f: The barber should lose, because his heart attack was an unforeseeable result of the prank.

Q938.L1t: CPR combines chest compressions and rescue breaths to keep blood and oxygen moving during cardiac arrest.
Q938.L2t: Effective adult chest compressions need adequate depth and a rate of about 100 to 120 per minute with minimal interruptions.
Q938.L3t: Compressions work by squeezing the heart between the sternum and the spine, so the body must not cushion or absorb the force and must lie level so each push goes straight down.
Q938.L4t: CPR works best when the patient lies level on their back on something rigid.
Q938.L2f: Adult chest compressions in CPR should be only about one centimeter deep.
Q938.L3f: Standard adult CPR requires rotating the body toward its left side so that blood keeps filling the heart during compressions.
Q938.L4f: The best CPR position is with the patient angled onto the left side to keep the heart perfused.

Q893.L1t: Burglary at common law requires breaking and entering the dwelling of another at night with the intent to commit a felony inside.
Q893.L2t: Voluntary intoxication can negate specific intent in a specific-intent crime like burglary, but only if the intoxication was severe enough to actually prevent forming that intent.
Q893.L3t: The two men discussed the plan, judged it a safe bet, picked out valuables, broke in, took the jewelry, and drove away, all of which shows purposeful, coordinated thinking and not a mind incapable of forming intent.
Q893.L4t: The defense will probably fail, because the facts show he was not so intoxicated that he could not form the intent to commit a felony inside.
Q893.L2f: Burglary is classed as a general-intent offense, so a defendant's mental state at the time of entry is not examined.
Q893.L3f: Under the law, any intoxication that alters a person's normal mental state, such as feeling drunk and aggressive, is enough to defeat the mens rea of a specific-intent crime.
Q893.L4f: The defense will likely succeed, because feeling drunk and aggressive was not his natural mental state, so he lacked the required mens rea.

Q1000.L1t: Women's participation in organized competitive athletics, including the Olympic Games, has grown a great deal since the early twentieth century.
Q1000.L2t: Elite women's world records have improved at a faster rate than men's records over recent decades, while men's records are still faster overall.
Q1000.L3t: A bigger pool of female athletes means more chances of finding rare, exceptionally talented individuals, and this pushes record performances up faster than in groups whose participation has already plateaued.
Q1000.L4t: The rapid improvement is mainly because many more women now take part in sport.
Q1000.L2f: Women's world records have improved at the same slow rate as men's records over recent decades.

Q1000.L4f: The rapid improvement is mainly because women can now run faster than men.

Q1007.L1t: Healthy skin is protected by a thin surface layer of natural oils and moisture that keeps it supple and acts as a barrier.
Q1007.L2t: Shampoos are formulated for hair and scalp, and they contain surfactants and detergents designed to remove sebum and grease from hair.
Q1007.L3t: The detergents in shampoo strip natural oils from the skin surface, and when used on the body they remove more of this protective lipid layer than the skin can easily replace.
Q1007.L4t: Shampoo should not be used on the skin because it can cause dryness of the skin.
Q1007.L2f: Shampoos are made with no detergents at all, and they are generally mild enough to be classed as emollients.
Q1007.L3f: Shampoo contains added silicones and conditioning oils that coat the skin in a slick film, which makes the shower floor and the skin itself unsafe and slippery.
Q1007.L4f: Shampoo should not be used on the skin because it is more slippery than soap or emollients.

Q975.L1t: Sodium bicarbonate is an alkalinising supplement that athletes sometimes take before high-intensity events.
Q975.L2t: During intense middle distance running, muscles produce large amounts of hydrogen ions that lower muscle pH and contribute to fatigue.
Q975.L3t: Bicarbonate taken before exercise raises blood pH and bicarbonate concentration, which steepens the gradient between muscle and blood so hydrogen ions move out of the working muscle faster.
Q975.L4t: Sodium bicarbonate helps by making the blood more alkaline and better buffered, so hydrogen ions leave the muscle more quickly.
Q975.L2f: Hydrogen ions produced during middle distance running are made mainly by the aerobic breakdown of fat and have little to do with muscle fatigue.
Q975.L3f: Sodium bicarbonate is a weak acid, so ingesting it lowers blood pH and buffering capacity, which pulls hydrogen ions out of the muscle along a steeper gradient.
Q975.L4f: Sodium bicarbonate helps by making the blood more acidic and less buffered, so hydrogen ions leave the muscle more quickly.

Q929.L1t: The Constitution divides power between the federal government and the states and gives Congress a defined list of enumerated powers.
Q929.L2t: Article I gives Congress the power to lay and collect taxes, and courts have long upheld taxes that apply to goods sold nationwide.
Q929.L3t: A tax that is applied to a product and raises money for the federal government falls within Congress's express taxing power, and that power does not depend on the product moving in interstate commerce or on the state being unwilling.
Q929.L4t: The tax is valid because Congress has the constitutional power to tax in order to raise revenue.
Q929.L2f: Under the Constitution, federal taxes on consumer goods may be imposed only when approved by a majority of state legislatures.
Q929.L3f: The key rule is that the supremacy clause is itself the source of Congress's power, so any federal law is valid simply because Congress enacted it and federal law outranks state law.
Q929.L4f: The tax is valid because the supremacy clause makes laws enacted by Congress constitutional.

Q399.L1t: Circulatory overload is a complication of intravenous fluid or blood transfusion therapy that nurses must monitor for.
Q399.L2t: Circulatory overload occurs when fluid is given too quickly or in too large a volume for the cardiovascular system to handle.
Q399.L3t: Excess fluid volume raises venous pressure and strains the heart and lungs, causing breathlessness, a fast heart rate, and visibly engorged neck veins.
Q399.L4t: Circulatory overload shows as shortness of breath, a rapid heart rate, and distended neck veins.
Q399.L2f: Circulatory overload is caused mainly by giving too little fluid too slowly, which leaves the vascular system depleted.
Q399.L3f: Circulatory overload reduces the body's circulating volume and heat production, so a careful reader would expect a fall in body temperature, a drop in blood pressure, and a slow pulse.
Q399.L4f: Circulatory overload shows as low body temperature, low blood pressure, and a slow heart rate.

Q887.L1t: Gastric motility is controlled by the autonomic nervous system and by hormones, and some drugs can speed up or slow down stomach emptying.
Q887.L2t: Prokinetic drugs increase coordinated contractions of the stomach and speed up gastric emptying, and they are sometimes used in gastroparesis.
Q887.L3t: This antibiotic is a macrolide that acts as an agonist at motilin receptors on gastric smooth muscle, so it triggers strong propulsive contractions in the stomach.
Q887.L4t: The macrolide antibiotic erythromycin is the drug on the list that can be used to enhance gastric motility.
Q887.L2f: Prokinetic drugs work mainly by blocking calcium channels in gastric smooth muscle, which is why they are used to treat gastroparesis.
Q887.L3f: This catecholamine stimulates adrenergic receptors in the gut wall to increase the force and frequency of gastric contractions, so it speeds up gastric emptying.
Q887.L4f: Adrenaline is the drug on the list that enhances gastric motility.

Q970.L1t: Federal courts decide evidentiary privileges between spouses under rules that grew out of the common law.
Q970.L2t: Federal law recognizes two separate spousal privileges: the adverse testimonial privilege, which belongs to the witness spouse, and the privilege for confidential marital communications.
Q970.L3t: Under Federal Rule of Evidence 501, privileges in federal criminal cases come from federal common law, and the confidential marital communications privilege can be asserted by the defendant even when the spouse is willing to testify.
Q970.L4t: The testimony should be excluded because the defendant can block a confidential statement made to his wife, even though she is willing to testify.
Q970.L2f: The federal marital communications privilege covers every statement between spouses, whether or not it was made in confidence.
Q970.L3f: Federal Rule of Evidence 501 tells federal courts in criminal cases to apply the privilege law of the state where the parties live, so the state's marital privilege rules control.
Q970.L4f: The testimony is excluded only if the law of the couple's home state recognizes a confidential marital communications privilege.

Q392.L1t: A speaking valve is a one-way valve fitted to a tracheostomy tube, and it is only used after a clinical assessment of the patient.
Q392.L2t: A speaking valve lets air in through the tube when the patient breathes in, and it closes on breathing out so that air is directed up through the larynx.
Q392.L3t: Because the valve shuts on breathing out, exhaled air has to pass around the tube and up through the upper airway, which only works if there is no inflated cuff blocking the space around the tube.
Q392.L4t: The cuff must be fully deflated before a speaking valve is fitted, so that the patient can breathe out around the tube.
Q392.L2f: A speaking valve is normally fitted straight after the tracheostomy is created, while the patient is still sedated in theatre.
Q392.L3f: Speaking valves are only safe once the stoma has fully matured, which is why a fixed waiting period after insertion is the key requirement before one can be used.
Q392.L4f: A speaking valve may only be used once seven days have passed since the tracheostomy tube was first inserted.

Q953.L1t: Blood components must be stored, handled and administered under strictly controlled conditions to keep recipients safe.
Q953.L2t: Red cell units are kept in a monitored blood bank fridge, and the time a unit may be out of controlled storage before transfusion is limited by local policy.
Q953.L3t: Once a unit has been out of controlled storage beyond the permitted time, its safety can no longer be guaranteed, so it must not be given or put back into general use, and the blood bank has to be told so that it can decide what happens to it and record it.
Q953.L4t: The unit should go back to the blood bank, with an explanation of why it is being returned.
Q953.L2f: Blood units must always be warmed to body temperature in a water bath before they are transfused, which is why they are taken out of the fridge early.
Q953.L3f: An out-of-time unit is classed as clinical waste that the ward is responsible for disposing of, and the empty bag is retained as the record of what happened.
Q953.L4f: The unit should be emptied in the sluice and the bag kept for records.

Q954.L1t: Urinary catheterization is an invasive procedure that is done with aseptic technique and attention to patient dignity and safety.
Q954.L2t: Before catheterizing, the nurse prepares the equipment, the environment and the patient, and checks that the sterile items are in date and intact.
Q954.L3t: Preparation covers things that affect the patient's own care and the safety of the procedure, such as agreement to treatment, hygiene and sterile equipment, and it does not include telling relatives, who have no part in the procedure itself.
Q954.L4t: Phoning the patient's next of kin is not a step that is done before catheterization.
Q954.L2f: Catheterization is a clean, non-sterile procedure, so equipment is not usually checked beforehand.
Q954.L3f: A competent adult's agreement is not needed for catheterization, because it is a routine nursing task covered by general admission consent.
Q954.L4f: Gaining the patient's consent is the step that is not done before catheterization.

Q916.L1t: Intravenous cannulae come in a range of sizes, and the gauge chosen depends on the patient and the reason for the infusion.
Q916.L2t: Gauge numbering is inverse, so a lower gauge number means a wider bore and a higher number means a finer needle.
Q916.L3t: A 14-16 gauge cannula is a very wide bore, which allows very fast flow of large volumes of fluid or blood, and this is needed when a patient is losing volume rapidly.
Q916.L4t: A 14-16 gauge needle is most likely to be used for trauma or burns patients.
Q916.L2f: Higher gauge numbers mean wider needles, so a 14-16 gauge needle is a fairly fine one.
Q916.L3f: Elderly patients have fragile, large and prominent veins that need the widest bore cannula to avoid collapse, so very low gauge numbers suit them best.
Q916.L4f: A 14-16 gauge needle is most likely to be used for elderly patients.

Q937.L1t: Morphine is an opioid analgesic derived from the opium poppy and used for moderate to severe pain.
Q937.L2t: Morphine acts mainly on mu-opioid receptors in the brain and spinal cord to reduce the perception of pain.
Q937.L3t: Opioid receptor activation in the central nervous system depresses neuronal activity, so morphine's central effects include drowsiness and a lowered level of consciousness rather than stimulation.
Q937.L4t: Morphine relieves pain but also produces sedation as a side effect.
Q937.L2f: Morphine is a synthetic compound first made in the 1990s and works by blocking prostaglandin synthesis in peripheral tissues.
Q937.L3f: Morphine acts as a central nervous system stimulant, so its pain relief comes with heightened wakefulness and arousal.
Q937.L4f: Morphine reduces pain and also increases alertness, so it is the stimulating analgesic.

Q922.L1t: Muscle contraction during exercise is powered by ATP, which is regenerated by several energy systems.
Q922.L2t: In high intensity exercise, ATP is used at a very high rate and is resynthesised by phosphocreatine breakdown and anaerobic glycolysis.
Q922.L3t: During intense exercise ADP and inorganic phosphate accumulate while ATP concentration is maintained, and the rate at which the cell can resupply ATP lags behind the rate at which contraction consumes it.
Q922.L4t: Fatigue in high intensity exercise arises when ATP resupply cannot keep pace with ATP demand.
Q922.L2f: Muscle cells hold large ATP stores that last for several minutes of maximal exercise before any other energy system is needed.
Q922.L3f: During high intensity exercise, ADP in the muscle cell is rapidly used up and its concentration drops, which stops ATP from being produced.
Q922.L4f: Fatigue in high intensity exercise is caused by a fall in the cell's ADP concentration.

Q907.L1t: In criminal law, the prosecution must prove every element of the charged offence beyond a reasonable doubt.
Q907.L2t: Intent is a mental state that is rarely proved directly and is usually shown through circumstantial evidence of what the defendant did.
Q907.L3t: A jury instruction that merely allows the jury to infer a fact from proven facts, without requiring it to do so and without shifting any burden to the defendant, leaves the prosecution's burden intact.
Q907.L4t: The instruction was proper because it only permitted the jury to infer intent, which the jury remained free to accept or reject.
Q907.L2f: Arson at common law required the burning of another person's dwelling, and intent was never an element that had to be proved.
Q907.L3f: The instruction told the jury it must find intent once it found that four matches were missing, which relieves the prosecution of proving that element.
Q907.L4f: The instruction was improper because the prosecution must prove every element of the crime beyond a reasonable doubt, and the instruction undermined that.

Q993.L1t: The Seventh Amendment preserves the right to a jury trial in federal civil cases that are legal in nature, and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 38 governs how that right is invoked.
Q993.L2t: Under Rule 38, a party can waive the right to a jury trial by failing to make a proper and timely demand.
Q993.L3t: Rule 38 lets a party demand a jury by serving a written demand no later than 14 days after the last pleading directed to the issue is served, and it also allows the demand to be made in a pleading itself.
Q993.L4t: The lawyer should include the jury demand in the complaint, which is filed and served at the start of the action, so the right is secured at the earliest possible point.
Q993.L2f: Patent infringement claims are equitable in nature, so federal courts historically tried them without a jury.
Q993.L3f: Under the federal rules, a jury demand is timely if it is raised orally with the court at the initial pretrial conference, since that is when the trial format is set.
Q993.L4f: The lawyer should wait and make the jury demand at the initial pretrial conference, because that is the proper time to secure a jury trial.

Q947.L1t: Pain is a subjective experience that is influenced by physical, emotional, and cultural factors, and it is a central concern in nursing and clinical care.
Q947.L2t: Pain assessment tools such as numeric rating scales and visual analogue scales were developed to help quantify what patients report about their pain.
Q947.L3t: Unlike blood pressure or temperature, pain has no laboratory test, scan, or instrument that can measure it directly, so clinicians have to depend on what the patient tells them.
Q947.L4t: The patient's self-report matters because staff have no objective way of measuring pain.
Q947.L2f: Pain scales are used only for patients who are unconscious, and conscious patients are never asked to rate their pain.
Q947.L3f: Studies consistently show that health care staff routinely rate a patient's pain as lower than the patient reports, which makes the patient's own rating necessary as a correction.
Q947.L4f: The patient's self-report matters because staff tend to underestimate how intense the patient's pain is.

Q992.L1t: Rape is a criminal offense defined by statute or common law, and the defenses available to a defendant depend on the mental state the offense requires.
Q992.L2t: Voluntary intoxication is a defense only to crimes that require a specific intent, and it is generally not a defense to crimes of general intent or recklessness.
Q992.L3t: Under the traditional rule, a defendant's mistaken belief that the victim consented can negate guilt only if the belief was honest and also reasonable, and the jury has found this belief was unreasonable.
Q992.L4t: The defendant should be found guilty because the victim did not consent and his belief that she consented was unreasonable.
Q992.L2f: At common law, rape required proof that the defendant specifically intended to cause the victim serious bodily harm.
Q992.L3f: A defendant who is voluntarily intoxicated is held only to the mental state he actually had, so intoxication may be used to negate any mental element, including the intent for general intent crimes.
Q992.L4f: The defendant should be found guilty because rape is a general intent crime, so his intoxication and honest belief do not matter.

Q876.L1t: Criminal homicide is divided into murder and manslaughter, and the degree depends on the defendant's mental state toward causing death.
Q876.L2t: Larceny by trick requires obtaining possession of property by fraud, while false pretenses requires obtaining title to property by a knowing false statement.
Q876.L3t: The woman handed over the $500 fee voluntarily as payment, intending to give the doctor ownership of the money and not merely possession, and the doctor acted without intent to kill or cause grievous harm but with reckless disregard for her life.
Q876.L4t: The doctor is guilty of manslaughter for the death and of false pretenses for getting the fee by lying about the pregnancy.
Q876.L2f: Manslaughter requires proof that the defendant specifically intended to kill the victim before the act.
Q876.L3f: The doctor lied to get the fee and to get her admitted, so deceiving the hospital while performing the surgery shows a malicious intent to kill, and the woman gave him only temporary possession of the fee, not title.
Q876.L4f: The doctor is guilty of murder for the death and of larceny by trick for obtaining the fee through the pregnancy lie.

Q902.L1t: Fluid balance in the body is the net result of intake and of losses through urine, stool, skin and breath.
Q902.L2t: Insensible losses are water losses from the skin and respiratory tract that cannot be seen or easily measured.
Q902.L3t: Insensible loss depends on evaporation from skin and airways and rises with fever, increased ventilation, and diarrhoea-type extra losses, whereas losing body mass over time through weight loss is not an evaporative route of water loss.
Q902.L4t: Excessive weight loss is not a cause of insensible loss.
Q902.L2f: Insensible losses are mostly measured directly by weighing the urine output of a patient each hour.
Q902.L3f: Unhumidified oxygen is delivered dry and so has no effect on the water that leaves the airways, meaning it cannot change evaporative respiratory loss.
Q902.L4f: Using unhumidified oxygen is the one thing that does not cause insensible loss.

Q905.L1t: Tort suits against government bodies depend on whether sovereign immunity applies and on what duties the entity owes.
Q905.L2t: Many jurisdictions have limited sovereign immunity so that governmental functions are protected while proprietary functions are not.
Q905.L3t: Maintaining a water main is a proprietary function of a municipal water department, and a duty to keep public ways safe from dangerous excavations is non-delegable, so hiring a contractor does not shield the department.
Q905.L4t: The estate will most probably win because immunity does not cover non-delegable proprietary duties.
Q905.L2f: Municipal water departments are given complete sovereign immunity for all their activities, including maintaining water mains.
Q905.L3f: The water department hired an independent contractor to do the repair, and a principal never owes any duty for dangerous work that is carried out by a contractor.
Q905.L4f: The estate will most probably lose because the water department is not liable for its independent contractor's negligence.

Q955.L1t: Hearsay is defined as an out-of-court statement offered to prove the truth of the matter it asserts, and the rules of evidence provide a number of exceptions to the general bar on such statements.
Q955.L2t: A witness may testify to what they personally heard, and the same words can be hearsay or non-hearsay depending on the purpose for which they are offered.
Q955.L3t: The plaintiff is relaying his son's words only to show that the windows shattered, which indicates how big the explosion was, and a statement offered for something other than its truth is not hearsay, so no exception is needed and the son's availability does not matter.
Q955.L4t: The testimony is admissible regardless of whether the son can testify, because it is not hearsay in the first place.
Q955.L2f: The excited utterance exception requires that a statement be made while the declarant was still under the stress of a startling event, and it applies only if the declarant is unavailable to testify.
Q955.L3f: The son's words are an out-of-court assertion offered for their truth, so they count as hearsay, and they come in only if they qualify as a spontaneous excited utterance, which is doubtful because a child's remark about shattered car windows could reflect reflection and deliberation.
Q955.L4f: The testimony is inadmissible, because the son's statement cannot qualify as an excited utterance given that it could be a product of reflection and deliberation.

Q909.L1t: Good oral hygiene in patients who cannot care for themselves is an important part of basic nursing care.
Q909.L2t: Mouth care products have been compared in studies, and some commonly used agents can dry or irritate the oral mucosa when used repeatedly.
Q909.L3t: The recommended agent for cleaning the mouth is the one that is plain, non-irritating, does not dry the mucosa and does not alter the oral environment, and glycerine with lemon is acidic and drying, which makes it unsuitable.
Q909.L4t: Plain water is the recommended agent for cleaning the mouth.
Q909.L2f: Mouth care for dependent patients is recommended at least once a week, and the choice of cleaning agent has no effect on oral mucosal comfort or dryness.
Q909.L3f: Lemon and glycerine swabs stimulate saliva, moisturise the mucosa and are the gentlest agent available, so guidelines favour them over other solutions for cleaning the mouth.
Q909.L4f: Lemon and glycerine swabs are the recommended choice for cleaning the mouth.

Q884.L1t: Diplopia, or double vision, is a symptom caused by misalignment of the visual axes, and it is assessed by examining eye movements and the cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles.
Q884.L2t: Binocular diplopia disappears when one eye is covered, whereas monocular diplopia persists in the affected eye and usually has an ocular cause.
Q884.L3t: In a squint the image from the deviated eye falls on a non-macular part of the retina and is projected to the opposite side, and the image of the paralysed eye is the less distinct one, so the image seen furthest out is the one belonging to the affected eye.
Q884.L4t: The outer image is always the false image seen in diplopia.
Q884.L2f: Diplopia always has a central cause and is never produced by a problem with the muscles or nerves of the eye itself.
Q884.L3f: The sixth cranial nerve supplies the lateral rectus, and its palsy leaves the medial rectus unopposed so the eye turns outwards, which is the picture of a divergent squint.
Q884.L4f: A sixth nerve palsy causes a divergent squint.

Q879.L1t: Muscular exercise draws on several energy systems, including phosphocreatine breakdown, anaerobic glycolysis and oxidative metabolism.
Q879.L2t: During maximal dynamic exercise, the contribution of oxidative metabolism to total ATP production rises steadily as the effort continues.
Q879.L3t: Studies of maximal effort show that anaerobic and aerobic sources supply about equal amounts of energy at roughly the one-minute mark, after which aerobic metabolism provides the larger share.
Q879.L4t: Maximal dynamic exercise becomes predominantly aerobic after about one minute.
Q879.L2f: During maximal dynamic exercise, oxidative metabolism contributes nothing to ATP production until the muscle's phosphocreatine stores are completely exhausted.
Q879.L3f: Studies of maximal effort show that aerobic and anaerobic sources only reach equal contributions after several minutes, since oxidative metabolism takes that long to ramp up.
Q879.L4f: Maximal dynamic exercise becomes predominantly aerobic only after about four minutes.

Q894.L1t: The hearsay rule excludes out-of-court statements offered for their truth unless they fall within a recognized exception or exclusion.
Q894.L2t: A statement made in a pleading filed in a prior lawsuit can be offered later in another proceeding, and its admissibility depends on who made it and who it is offered against.
Q894.L3t: The rider is offering the roommate's own earlier statement against the roommate, who is a party to the current suit, and the roommate made it himself in his own complaint.
Q894.L4t: The complaint is admissible as an admission by a party-opponent.
Q894.L2f: A pleading filed in a prior lawsuit is never treated as a statement of the party who filed it, because pleadings are written by lawyers and not by the parties.
Q894.L3f: The complaint was made in an earlier judicial proceeding, and the rider is offering it in a later trial to show what the roommate swore to under oath on the same factual issue.
Q894.L4f: The complaint is admissible under the former testimony exception to the hearsay rule.

Q978.L1t: Hospital discharge planning aims to make sure patients leave hospital safely and that their continuing care is arranged.
Q978.L2t: The Department of Health issued guidance in 2004 recommending a checklist to support safe and well-coordinated hospital discharge.
Q978.L3t: The 2004 guidance stresses that the patient should be included in completing the checklist, together with the nurse and the ward clerk who handle the practical arrangements.
Q978.L4t: The nurse, the patient and the ward clerk should complete the form.
Q978.L2f: The 2004 Department of Health discharge checklist was intended only for patients being discharged from intensive care units and was not meant for general wards.
Q978.L3f: The 2004 guidance says the checklist is an administrative record that should be completed by hospital staff alone, with the ward clerk and the consultant working alongside the nurse and the patient left out of it.
Q978.L4f: The nurse, the ward clerk and the consultant should complete the form.
